newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-CHANG CRUSHES AGASSI TO REACH U.S. OPEN FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CHANG CRUSHES AGASSI TO REACH U.S. OPEN FINAL.

text.p: Michael Chang crushed Andre Agassi at his own game on Saturday to claim a shockingly easy straight sets victory and a place in the U.S. Open final.

Chang overwhelmed Agassi, the game's premier returner, with his service and also outplayed the renowned backcourt slugger from the baseline to administer a 6-3 6-2 6-2 beating in the semifinals at the National Tennis Centre.

"Things just really went well for me. Today everything clicked," said the second-seeded Chang, who finished off the one hour 53-minute contest with a 116 mile-per-hour (187 kph) ace, his 16th of the match.
The second-seeded Chang will meet the winner of the day's other semifinal between top-seeded defending champion Pete Sampras and fourth seed Goran Ivanisevic.
Earlier, Steffi Graf fought off five set points in the opening set on her way to a 7-5 6-3 victory over 15-year-old Martina Hingis of Switzerland.
The top-seeded defending champion from Germany will face Monica Seles in Sunday's final, a re-match of last year's championship showdown.

Chang, who had lost to Agassi in straight sets in the hard court finals in Cincinnati earlier this month, trailed in their career series 11-6 and had twice been defeated at past Opens by his longtime rival.
But Chang, who had the easiest path to the semifinals of any player, continued his smooth ride into his first Open final with astonishing ease against the sixth-seeded Agassi.
"Although Andre has dropped in the rankings, today I was still the underdog," said Chang. "My ranking is higher but I think people expected Andre to beat me today.
"He's got a winning record against me and he's beaten me here in the past. But it was one of those days when everything happened to go my way."
Chang, the Australian Open runner-up who is ranked third in the world, could become the new world number one with a victory in Sunday's final.
Agassi said the windy conditions combined with Chang's challenging attack made it hard for him to find his rhythm.
"He picked up his service and I never really found my game," said Agassi. "He forced me to press a little bit.
"The conditions didn't lend themselves either to find your rhythm and Michael Chang is a hard player to find your rhythm against. It wasn't good."
Chang was too good on the day for Agassi.

The 24-year-old Chang was a step quicker than Agassi in getting to balls early and dictating points. He hit the ball more crisply and mixed up his serves brilliantly -- spinning some and bashing others to the bewilderment of the flamboyant Las Vegan.
"I didn't put any pressure on his second serve so he kept on going for his first serve and he found his range," said Agassi, whose black-and-blue outfit befitted the beating he suffered.

"Usually I'm taking good clean shots but I couldn't even make good errors on his second serves today," moaned Agassi. "I wanted to keep hitting my shots and hoping I'd find it, but I was not even close."
Agassi committed 45 unforced errors to just 23 for Chang, whose ace total was times as many as Agassi's.

Facing his first seeded opponent of the tournament, Chang took advantage of a poor service game from Agassi to break for a 5-3 lead in the opening set. He held at 15 to close the set, winning 12 of the last 15 points contested.
In the second game of the second set, Agassi battled fiercely to break Chang, showing signs of fire by running around his backhand to lash forehand winners down the line.
But Chang fended him off, uncorking three aces during their seven deuces, and survived two break points to hold serve.
Chang turned up the pressure on Agassi in the next game and cashed in on his fourth break point when his frustrated foe whipped a forehand long.
Chang broke again in the seventh game to lead 5-2, then ended the set with a sizzling ace.
The rampaging Chang galloped to a 5-1 lead in the third set and never allowed Agassi an opening to fight his way back.
He reached 40-0 in the last game with his 15th ace, and two points later ended it with number 16.

Chang, who won the French Open at the tender age of 17, finally got back to a Grand Slam final again last year at Roland Garros and reached the Australian Open final earlier this year, losing to Boris Becker.
Now he is knocking at the Grand Slam door again.
"I'm pretty excited," Chang said about his Sunday prospects. "I think I have a pretty good shot."
